zh.title: 年利润超过400万美元后，他却说：我不想把一人公司 OPC 做大
zh.excerpt: Justin Welsh 的选择让我重新问自己：如果一个机会真的成功，它会让我过上想要的生活吗？
zh.content:
![SMALL BY DESIGN · $4M WAS NOT THE POINT. · AI 辅助概念视觉，非 Justin Welsh 肖像](/assets/notes/2026-09-21-justin-small-by-design/cover.png)

今天，我在「虾子曰·昨日世界」看到一张海报。

画面里最大的数字是：**400万美元利润。**

主人公叫 Justin Welsh。他把自己的销售与创业经验做成课程、咨询、内容赞助和订阅产品，经营着一家几乎没有正式员工的一人公司。

这已经足够吸引人了。

![在「虾子曰·昨日世界」看到的 OPC 一人公司海报 · 它让我顺着链接，继续读到了数字背后的选择](/assets/notes/2026-09-21-justin-small-by-design/poster.png)

但我顺着网站（[xiazishuo.com](https://xiazishuo.com/)）提供的链接，找到他的独立站，读完他最近写的《What if it works?》，发现真正打动我的并不是那个数字。

恰恰相反。

Justin 在文章里说，2024 年是他业务的高峰，全年利润超过 400 万美元。但他可能再也不会达到这个数字，也没有兴趣为了回到那里，重新扩张团队、增加会议和管理工作。

一个把一人公司做到这种规模的人，最新的思考居然是：

> 如果一个机会真的成功了，我会因此得到自己想要的生活吗？

这比“怎样赚到400万美元”有意思得多。

![Justin Welsh 文章《What if it works?》· 图片来自作者独立站，文章发表于 2026 年 9 月 12 日](/assets/notes/2026-09-21-justin-small-by-design/what-if-it-works.png)

## 01 / FIELD NOTE｜在成为“一人公司样板”之前，他先被工作击倒过

Justin 并不是一开始就想当创作者。

他做了十多年销售，后来进入 SaaS 创业公司，帮助两家公司成长到超过 10 亿美元估值。在 PatientPop 任职期间，他带领过上百人的销售团队，也经历了公司高速增长。

从简历看，这是一条标准的成功曲线：职位越来越高，团队越来越大，数字越来越漂亮。

身体却先给出了另一份报表。

按照 Justin 自己的回忆，2018 年 12 月 16 日，他经历了一次严重的惊恐发作。长期工作压力、失控感、睡眠不足以及不健康的生活方式叠加到一起，他一度以为自己快要死了，妻子叫来了急救人员。

第二天，他提出离开管理岗位。为了完成交接，他又工作了大约九个月，随后正式结束了自己的科技公司高管生涯。

这不是一次潇洒的“裸辞故事”。

他当时有房贷，也不知道自己的新事业能不能成立。后来疫情到来，他甚至怀疑，离职创业可能是一个代价昂贵的错误。

但这次惊恐发作迫使他面对一个更难的问题：

**如果所谓的成功，正在把生活变成自己不想要的样子，它还算成功吗？**

## 02 / FIELD NOTE｜他没有先做产品，而是先把经验写出来

离职后，Justin 没有立即设计一门宏大的课程，也没有先画商业模式画布。

他从最普通的一件事开始：持续写自己真正懂的东西。

他在 LinkedIn 分享 SaaS 销售、团队建设和创业经验。一开始没有精密的内容策略，只是反复表达、观察哪些问题会引起回应，再沿着那些真实反馈继续写。

接着，事情一步步发生：

有创业者向他请教销售问题，他开始做咨询；

很多人追问他如何经营 LinkedIn，他把自己的方法做成了一个售价 50 美元的小课程；

他发现自己每周都在制作内容模板，于是把模板做成每月订阅；

有了持续阅读的受众，他开始写 newsletter，也加入内容赞助；

重复出现的问题，逐渐变成课程、模板、订阅和新的内容。


这条路径没有“灵光一现”的戏剧性。

它更像一个很朴素的循环：

**写出经验 → 吸引同类 → 回答问题 → 发现需求 → 做成产品 → 再从用户反馈里继续写。**

他不是先猜一个市场，再努力找人购买；而是先在公开表达中建立信任，再把重复解决的问题产品化。

Justin 在 2025 年公开的复盘里说，他的业务用了五年九个月累计突破 1000 万美元收入；产品、咨询、赞助、订阅和社区构成了主要收入来源。当时他公布的利润率约为 89%，并称整个过程没有投放付费广告。

不过，“一人公司”也不等于一个人完成所有事情。他同样说明，妻子给了他很多帮助，外包虚拟助理处理客服，需要时也会与专业人士合作。

他真正拒绝的，是重新建立一套需要自己长期管理的员工组织。

## 03 / FIELD NOTE｜最厉害的不是收入，而是他关掉过赚钱的业务

很多人讲一人公司，会讲“轻资产”“高利润率”“内容复利”。

Justin 的经历里，我更在意另一件事：**他会主动关掉不符合生活目标的生意。**

他曾经经营一个每月收入约 1.5 万美元的创作者社区。商业上，它并不失败；问题是，社区让他感觉自己必须一直守在 Slack 里。

这正是他离开上一份工作的原因。

于是，社区上线 15 个月后，他把它关掉了。

这个决定放在 Excel 里可能很难解释。一个正在赚钱的产品，为什么不继续做大？

但如果把“想过怎样的生活”也写进报表，它就突然合理了。

Justin 在 2020 年给自己写下六条边界：

1. 不管理员工；

2. 每周工作不超过 30 小时；

3. 尽量把星期五完整留出来；

4. 一天不超过两场会议；

5. 每场会议不超过 45 分钟；

6. 工作不侵占与家人相处的夜晚和周末。


![THE RULES · 他为自己写下的六条经营边界 · 配图为 AI 辅助创作的概念视觉](/assets/notes/2026-09-21-justin-small-by-design/rules.png)

所以，当别人劝他投广告、招内容团队、做会员、办活动时，他考虑的不只是“能不能多赚一百万美元”。

他还会继续问：如果这件事非常成功，我每天将被迫做什么？

一个机会可能完全按照计划奏效，却把你送进一家自己根本不想经营的公司。

## 04 / FIELD NOTE｜一人公司，不是把自己变成十个人

我们很容易把一人公司理解成另一种极限挑战：一个人写内容、做产品、回客服、剪视频、投广告、做财务，最好还能顺手把服务器修了。

结果是，公司只有一个人，组织病却一样不少。会议变成待办清单，老板和员工都住在同一个脑子里，而且谁也下不了班。

Justin Welsh 的案例提醒我，一人公司的重点并不是“什么都自己干”。

而是用内容、软件、数字产品和外部协作，把同一项能力交付很多次，同时保留决定公司边界的权力。

他的核心资产也不是某一门课程。

真正持续复利的，是同一个主题下不断积累的内容、读者信任、邮件关系，以及对受众问题越来越准确的理解。产品可以变化，渠道可以变化，这些资产却能带着他进入下一次尝试。

这和“做一个爆款，然后躺着赚钱”是两回事。

截至 2025 年的那次复盘，他说自己已经写了超过 5000 条内容，经历了许多担心和失眠的日子。他也明确提醒读者：自己是一个少数样本，创作者生意很难，他的路径不能被照搬。

海报上的数字很大，背后的时间却很长。

## 05 / FIELD NOTE｜比“我要赚多少钱”更早的问题

读完 Justin 的故事，我没有立刻想去复制他的课程、newsletter 或销售漏斗。

我更想先写一张自己的清单：

我愿意长期重复做的工作是什么？

我不希望被什么事情占满？

一周工作多少小时，仍然觉得生活属于自己？

哪些收入看起来不错，却会把我重新带回不喜欢的状态？

如果一个机会真的成功，它会给我的日常增加什么？


很多商业计划先写市场、产品、渠道和收入。

也许还应该多一页：**我希望这家公司最终让我怎样生活。**

Justin Welsh 最值得介绍的，并不是他把一人公司做到了多大的数字。

而是经历过一次失控以后，他开始反过来设计公司：先确定自己不要什么，再决定什么样的增长值得接受。

收入当然重要。

但一家公司最好的版本，未必是它赚到最多钱的版本。

也可能是每天早上醒来，你仍然愿意亲自经营它的那个版本。

## 06 / FIELD NOTE｜我的答案：一休 · 不二 · 三慢

Justin 的经历让我想到，工作和生活从来不会永远停在高峰。真正重要的，也许不是设法避开所有低谷，而是在变化里仍然知道怎样照顾自己、理解自己，也不失去继续创造的能力。

这也是我越来越确定的一种生活态度：

**我们愿陪伴彼此走过低谷与高峰，探索身心健康的工作与生活方式；真实面对自己与世界，善待自己、他人与生命，并在创造和欣赏中活出生命之美。**

**一休不二三慢**

**一休：**先照顾身体，安顿情绪，再继续前行。

**不二：**不评判，没有好坏对错，接纳高峰与低谷，拥抱完整而非完美。

**三慢：**慢下来，慢慢来，慢慢成为。

**如水：**向内扎根，向外流动；顺应变化，不失本心。


### 资料说明 · 2026-09-21

本文数据与经历主要来自 Justin Welsh 的公开自述；相关收入、利润与受众数字未经本文独立审计。

[1] [What if it works?](https://justinwelsh.me/essays/what-if-it-works) · 2026-09-12

[2] [My complete $10M journey](https://justinwelsh.me/essays/my-10m-journey) · 2025-06-07

[3] [My $4.8M Social Media Sales Funnel](https://justinwelsh.me/essays/my-million-dollar-social-media-sales-funnel) · 2023-10-14

[4] [Justin Welsh 关于 2018 年惊恐发作的公开回忆](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/justinwelsh_on-december-16th-2018-i-had-a-massive-panic-activity-7019652895839014912-5IUZ)

线索海报来自[「虾子曰·昨日世界」](https://xiazishuo.com/)。封面及规则图由 AI 辅助创作；人物为概念形象，并非 Justin Welsh 肖像。

en.label: Field Notes · 10
en.title: After More Than $4 Million in Annual Profit, He Says: I Do Not Want a Bigger One-Person Business
en.excerpt: Justin Welsh’s choices raise a different question: if an opportunity succeeds, will it give me the life I want?
en.content:
![Small by Design · $4M Was Not the Point · AI-assisted concept image, not a portrait of Justin Welsh](/assets/notes/2026-09-21-justin-small-by-design/cover.png)

Today, I came across a poster in *Xiazi · Yesterday’s World*.

The largest number on it was **$4 million in profit**.

The person behind that number is Justin Welsh. He has turned his experience in sales and entrepreneurship into courses, consulting, content sponsorships, and subscription products, running a one-person business with almost no formal employees.

That alone is enough to catch your attention.

![The original Chinese OPC poster I found in Xiazi · Yesterday’s World. It led me to read about the choices behind the numbers.](/assets/notes/2026-09-21-justin-small-by-design/poster.png)

But after following the link on [xiazishuo.com](https://xiazishuo.com/) to his own website and reading his recent essay, *What if it works?*, I realized that the number was not what moved me.

Quite the opposite.

Justin writes that 2024 was his business’s peak, with more than $4 million in annual profit. He may never reach that figure again, and he has no interest in rebuilding a team, adding meetings, and taking on management work to get back there.

Someone who has built a one-person business on that scale is now asking a different question:

> If an opportunity really works out, will it give me the life I want?

That interests me far more than “How do I make $4 million?”

![Justin Welsh’s essay What if it works? · Image from his own website; published September 12, 2026](/assets/notes/2026-09-21-justin-small-by-design/what-if-it-works.png)

## 01 / FIELD NOTE｜Before he became a model solopreneur, work had knocked him down

Justin did not begin by wanting to be a creator.

He spent more than a decade in sales before joining SaaS startups, helping two companies grow to valuations above $1 billion. At PatientPop, he led a sales team of more than a hundred people through rapid growth.

On a résumé, it looks like the standard curve of success: a higher title, a bigger team, better numbers.

His body was producing a different report.

According to his own account, he suffered a severe panic attack on December 16, 2018. Prolonged work pressure, a loss of control, insufficient sleep, and unhealthy habits had accumulated. At one point he thought he was dying, and his wife called emergency responders.

The next day, he asked to leave his management role. He stayed for roughly nine more months to complete the handover, then brought his career as a technology executive to an end.

This was not a carefree story about quitting a job.

He had a mortgage and no certainty that his new business would work. When the pandemic arrived, he even wondered whether leaving to work for himself had been an expensive mistake.

But the panic attack forced him to confront a harder question:

**If what we call success is turning life into something we do not want, is it still success?**

## 02 / FIELD NOTE｜He started by writing about his experience, before building a product

After leaving, Justin did not immediately design an ambitious course or start with a business model canvas.

He began with something ordinary: consistently writing about what he actually knew.

On LinkedIn, he shared his experience in SaaS sales, team building, and entrepreneurship. There was no elaborate content strategy at first. He kept expressing his ideas, watched which questions drew responses, and used that real feedback to decide what to write next.

Then things happened step by step.

Founders asked him for sales advice, so he began consulting.

People kept asking how he used LinkedIn, so he turned his method into a small $50 course.

He noticed that he was making content templates every week, so he offered them as a monthly subscription.

With an audience that read him regularly, he started a newsletter and added sponsorships.

Recurring questions gradually became courses, templates, subscriptions, and more content.

There is no dramatic flash of inspiration in this path.

It looks more like a simple cycle:

**Write about experience → Attract people with similar interests → Answer questions → Discover needs → Make products → Keep writing from customer feedback.**

He did not first guess at a market and then search for people to buy. He built trust by sharing his thinking in public, then made products out of problems he repeatedly helped people solve.

In his public retrospective in 2025, Justin said his business had passed $10 million in cumulative revenue over five years and nine months. Products, consulting, sponsorships, subscriptions, and a community were the main sources of that revenue. He reported a profit margin of roughly 89% and said he had used no paid advertising throughout that period.

“One-person business” does not mean doing everything alone. He also explained that his wife helped extensively, an outsourced virtual assistant handled customer service, and he worked with specialists when needed.

What he rejected was rebuilding an employee organization that he would have to manage over the long term.

## 03 / FIELD NOTE｜What impresses me most is that he has closed profitable businesses

People often describe one-person businesses in terms of low overhead, high margins, and the compounding value of content.

Something else in Justin’s experience matters more to me: **he will close a business that does not fit the life he wants.**

He once ran a creator community generating about $15,000 in monthly revenue. Commercially, it was not a failure. The problem was that it made him feel he had to be in Slack all the time.

That was precisely what he had left his previous job to escape.

So, 15 months after launching the community, he shut it down.

The decision may be difficult to explain in a spreadsheet. Why not keep growing a product that is making money?

Add “the life I want to lead” to that spreadsheet, and it suddenly makes sense.

In 2020, Justin wrote down six boundaries for himself:

1. Do not manage employees.

2. Work no more than 30 hours a week.

3. Keep Fridays as free as possible.

4. Have no more than two meetings a day.

5. Keep each meeting to 45 minutes or less.

6. Protect evenings and weekends with family from work.

![The Rules · Six boundaries for his business · AI-assisted concept illustration](/assets/notes/2026-09-21-justin-small-by-design/rules.png)

When people encourage him to buy ads, hire a content team, build a membership, or run events, he considers more than whether he could make another million dollars.

He also asks: if this becomes very successful, what will I have to do every day?

An opportunity can work exactly as planned and still leave you running a company you never wanted.

## 04 / FIELD NOTE｜A one-person company should not turn you into ten people

It is easy to treat a one-person company as another endurance challenge: write content, build products, answer customers, edit videos, run ads, manage the accounts, and ideally fix the server along the way.

The company has only one person, yet it inherits plenty of organizational problems. Meetings become to-do lists. The boss and the employee live in the same head, and neither gets to clock out.

Justin Welsh’s experience reminds me that the point is not to do absolutely everything yourself.

It is to use content, software, digital products, and outside collaboration to deliver the same capability many times, while keeping the right to decide where your company’s boundaries lie.

His core asset is not any single course, either.

What keeps compounding is the content accumulated around a consistent subject, readers’ trust, relationships through email, and an increasingly accurate understanding of the audience’s problems. Products and channels can change. Those assets can travel with him into the next experiment.

That is a different proposition from making one hit product and then earning money in your sleep.

By the time of that 2025 retrospective, he said he had written more than 5,000 pieces of content and lived through plenty of worry and sleepless nights. He also explicitly warned readers that he is an unusual case, that a creator business is difficult, and that his path cannot simply be copied.

The numbers on the poster are large. The time behind them is long.

## 05 / FIELD NOTE｜A question to ask before “How much do I want to earn?”

After reading Justin’s story, my immediate response was not to copy his courses, newsletter, or sales funnel.

I wanted to write a list of my own:

What work am I willing to repeat over the long term?

What do I not want filling my days?

How many hours can I work each week and still feel that my life belongs to me?

Which sources of income look attractive but would return me to a state I dislike?

If an opportunity succeeds, what will it add to my everyday life?

Many business plans begin with markets, products, channels, and revenue.

Perhaps they need another page: **How do I want this company to let me live?**

The most worthwhile part of Justin Welsh’s story is not the scale of the numbers he has achieved.

It is that, after experiencing a loss of control, he began designing his company in reverse: first identify what he does not want, then decide which kinds of growth are worth accepting.

Income matters, of course.

But the best version of a company may not be the version that makes the most money.

It may be the one you still want to run yourself when you wake up each morning.

## 06 / FIELD NOTE｜My answer: Yixiu · Buer · Sanman

Justin’s experience reminds me that work and life will never remain at their peaks forever. What matters may be less about avoiding every low point than about knowing how to care for ourselves, understand ourselves, and keep creating through change.

This is an attitude toward life that I am becoming more certain of:

> We hope to accompany one another through life’s lows and highs, exploring ways of working and living that support both body and mind; to face ourselves and the world honestly, treat ourselves, others, and all life with kindness, and discover life’s beauty through creating and appreciating.

**Yixiu · Buer · Sanman**

**Yixiu — Rest:** Care for the body and settle the emotions before moving forward.

**Buer — Non-duality:** Without judgment or dividing experience into good and bad, right and wrong, accept both highs and lows. Embrace wholeness rather than perfection.

**Sanman — Slow down:** Slow down, take your time, and become yourself gradually.

**Like water:** Put down roots within and flow outward. Adapt to change without losing your center.

### Sources · September 21, 2026

The figures and experiences discussed here come primarily from Justin Welsh’s public accounts. Revenue, profit, and audience figures have not been independently audited for this essay.

[1] [What if it works?](https://justinwelsh.me/essays/what-if-it-works) · September 12, 2026.

[2] [My complete $10M journey](https://justinwelsh.me/essays/my-10m-journey) · June 7, 2025.

[3] [My $4.8M Social Media Sales Funnel](https://justinwelsh.me/essays/my-million-dollar-social-media-sales-funnel) · October 14, 2023.

[4] [Justin Welsh’s public account of his panic attack in 2018](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/justinwelsh_on-december-16th-2018-i-had-a-massive-panic-activity-7019652895839014912-5IUZ).

The poster that prompted this essay comes from [Xiazi · Yesterday’s World](https://xiazishuo.com/). The cover and rules illustration were created with AI assistance. The figure on the cover is a conceptual character, not a portrait of Justin Welsh.
